## Why Survey Language Matters

<p class="lead">
Marketing surveys are not neutral. The words we use shape how customers think, what identity they perform, and which trade-offs they notice.
</p>

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<h3>Traditional survey wording</h3>
<ul>
<li>"Would you buy this?"</li>
<li>"How important is this feature?"</li>
<li>"What would you pay?"</li>
<li>"Rate this 1–10."</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div>
<h3>Choice-based survey wording</h3>
<ul>
<li>"Which option would you choose?"</li>
<li>"Which is most and least important?"</li>
<li>"Would you buy at this price?"</li>
<li>"Which bundle feels worth it?"</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>

<div class="callout compact">
<p><span class="highlight">Main idea:</span> Better marketing surveys do not just ask for preferences. They design situations where preferences are <em>revealed through choices</em>.</p>
</div>

<div class="three-col compact-row">
<div>
<h4>Framing</h4>
<p>Language changes what people notice.</p>
</div>
<div>
<h4>Identity</h4>
<p>Answers reflect how people want to appear.</p>
</div>
<div>
<h4>Trade-offs</h4>
<p>Better questions make sacrifice unavoidable.</p>
</div>
</div>

<p class="source">
Sources:
<a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.1086/209535" target="_blank">Bettman, Luce & Payne</a>;
<a href="https://sites.socsci.uci.edu/~bskyrms/bio/readings/tversky_k_heuristics_biases.pdf" target="_blank">Tversky & Kahneman</a>;
</p>


## Conjoint: Building a Realistic Shopping Task

<p class="lead">
Conjoint changes the question from <span class="bad">"What features do you like?"</span> to <span class="good">"Which product bundle would you choose?"</span>
</p>

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<h3>How conjoint is constructed</h3>
<ul>
<li>Choose product <strong>attributes</strong></li>
<li>Define <strong>levels</strong> for each attribute</li>
<li>Build choice tasks from different combinations</li>
<li>Randomize and balance screens</li>
<li>Include a <strong>none option</strong> when realistic</li>
<li>Estimate <strong>part-worth utilities</strong> for each level</li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="option-box">

<h3>Example: Subscription bundle</h3>

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Attribute</th>
<th>Option A</th>
<th>Option B</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Price</td>
<td>$49/mo</td>
<td>$59/mo</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Delivery</td>
<td>Fast</td>
<td>Standard</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Support</td>
<td>Basic</td>
<td>Premium</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Packaging</td>
<td>Standard</td>
<td>Eco-friendly</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<p class="good">Which option would you choose? Or neither?</p>

</div>
</div>

<div class="callout compact">
<p><span class="highlight">Why "none" matters:</span> without it, respondents may be forced to choose a product they would never actually buy.</p>
</div>

<p class="source">
Sources: <a href="https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/publications/conjoint-analysis-marketing-new-developments-implications-research" target="_blank">Green & Srinivasan</a>.
</p>


## Why Conjoint Works: Trade-Offs Over Wish Lists

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<h3>Compared with direct surveys</h3>
<p>Direct questions isolate features:</p>
<ul>
<li>"Do you like fast delivery?"</li>
<li>"Is sustainability important?"</li>
<li>"Would you pay more?"</li>
<li>"What is your ideal product?"</li>
</ul>
<p class="bad">Problem: customers can want everything in theory.</p>
</div>

<div>
<h3>Conjoint forces realistic compromise</h3>
<p>Choice tasks combine positives and negatives:</p>
<ul>
<li>Fast shipping, but higher price</li>
<li>Eco packaging, but slower delivery</li>
<li>Premium support, but less convenience</li>
<li>Better brand, but fewer features</li>
</ul>
<p class="good">Result: marketers estimate what people actually give up for each feature.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="three-col compact-row">
<div>
<h4>Product</h4>
<p>Which features create value?</p>
</div>

<div>
<h4>Price</h4>
<p>What are people willing to pay?</p>
</div>

<div>
<h4>Segmentation</h4>
<p>Which groups value different bundles?</p>
</div>
</div>

<p class="arrow">Choice tasks   →   part-worth utilities   →   willingness to pay   → product and price decisions</p>

<p class="source">
Sources:
<a href="https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/publications/conjoint-analysis-marketing-new-developments-implications-research" target="_blank">Green & Srinivasan</a>
</p>


## The Psychology Behind Conjoint

<p class="lead">
Conjoint works because it transforms vague stated preferences into structured, multi-attribute choice behavior.
</p>

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<h3>Psychological theories</h3>

<div class="theory-card">
<strong>Multi-Attribute Utility Theory</strong>
<p>Products are bundles of attributes. Total value comes from the perceived value of each attribute level.</p>
</div>

<div class="theory-card">
<strong>Theory of Conjoint Measurement</strong>
<p>Qualitative judgments like "I prefer A to B" can be translated into numerical preference scales.</p>
</div>

<div class="theory-card">
<strong>Random Utility Theory</strong>
<p>Choice has a systematic part we can model and a random part we cannot fully observe.</p>
</div>

</div>

<div>
<h3>How conjoint uses them</h3>
<ul>
<li>Varies attributes and levels across tasks</li>
<li>Estimates part-worth utilities from choices</li>
<li>Treats price as one attribute among many</li>
<li>Models imperfect but predictable choice behavior</li>
<li>Reduces vague self-reporting by forcing bundle-level decisions</li>
</ul>
<p class="good">The survey does not ask people to explain their utility function. It infers it from choices.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="callout compact">
<p><span class="highlight">Bias mitigation:</span> social desirability is weaker when sustainability, price, brand, and convenience are bundled together. Respondents must trade off the full package.</p>
</div>

<p class="source">
Sources:
<a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.1086/209535" target="_blank">Bettman, Luce & Payne</a>;
<a href="https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/publications/conjoint-analysis-marketing-new-developments-implications-research" target="_blank">Green & Srinivasan</a>
</p>



## MaxDiff: Building a Prioritization Task

<p class="lead">
MaxDiff changes the question from <span class="bad">"How important is each item?"</span> to <span class="good">"Which is most and least important?"</span>
</p>

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<h3>How MaxDiff is constructed</h3>
<ul>
<li>Start with a long list of features, claims, or benefits</li>
<li>Show small sets of <strong>3–6 items</strong></li>
<li>Ask for the <strong>most</strong> and <strong>least</strong> preferred</li>
<li>Repeat across multiple screens</li>
<li>Balance item exposure and pairings</li>
<li>Estimate a preference score for every item</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div>
<h3>Example: Feature priorities</h3>
<div class="feature-card most"><p><span class="good">MOST</span>: Lower price</p></div>
<div class="feature-card"><p>Better battery life</p></div>
<div class="feature-card"><p>Better camera</p></div>
<div class="feature-card least"><p><span class="bad">LEAST</span>: Brand reputation</p></div>
</div>
</div>

<div class="callout compact">
<p><span class="highlight">Key difference from rating scales:</span> respondents cannot mark every feature as "very important." They must prioritize.</p>
</div>

<p class="source">
Sources:
<a href="https://www.qualtrics.com/support/conjoint-project/getting-started-conjoints/getting-started-maxdiff/maxdiff-analysis-white-paper/" target="_blank">Qualtrics MaxDiff overview</a>.
</p>



## The Psychology Behind MaxDiff

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<h3>Psychological theories</h3>

<div class="theory-card">
<strong>Thurstonian Scaling</strong>
<p>When people compare items, each item creates an underlying psychological value that can be recovered from repeated judgments.</p>
</div>

<div class="theory-card">
<strong>Elimination by Aspects</strong>
<p>People simplify complex choices by focusing on attributes that matter and eliminating weaker options.</p>
</div>

<div class="theory-card">
<strong>Random Utility Theory</strong>
<p>People choose the option or pair with the highest perceived utility difference, plus some noise.</p>
</div>

</div>
<div>
<h3>How MaxDiff uses them</h3>
<ul>
<li>Asks for extremes because best/worst is easier than exact ranking</li>
<li>Breaks long lists into small sets to reduce cognitive load</li>
<li>Forces trade-offs to prevent "everything is important"</li>
<li>Removes scale-use bias by avoiding 1–10 ratings</li>
<li>Produces a relative hierarchy of preferences</li>
</ul>
<p class="good">MaxDiff works because people are better at comparative judgment than absolute scoring.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="callout compact">
<p><span class="highlight">Core principle:</span> MaxDiff turns psychological comparison into marketing data.</p>
</div>

<p class="source">
Sources:
<a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022249611000964" target="_blank">Marley & Louviere / best-worst choice models</a>;
<a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022249672900119" target="_blank">Tversky, Elimination by Aspects</a>
</p>



## Conclusion: Better Surveys Create Better Segments

<p class="lead">
Conjoint and MaxDiff work because they turn vague self-reporting into structured choice behavior — and structured choices reveal how different customers actually value things.
</p>

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<h3>Weak survey design gives...</h3>
<ul>
<li>Inflated purchase intent</li>
<li>Vague ratings where everything scores high</li>
<li>"Everything is important"</li>
<li>Averages that hide meaningful differences</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div>
<h3>Choice-based survey design gives...</h3>
<ul>
<li>Realistic trade-offs</li>
<li>Part-worth utilities</li>
<li>Willingness to pay estimates</li>
<li>Preference scores</li>
<li>Preference-based segments</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>

<div class="three-col compact-row">
<div>
<h4>Price-sensitive</h4>
<p>Responds to value language and low-price framing.</p>
</div>
<div>
<h4>Quality-seeking</h4>
<p>Responds to performance language and feature detail.</p>
</div>
<div>
<h4>Identity-driven</h4>
<p>Responds to lifestyle language and brand signals.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="callout">
<p class="big">Good marketing surveys do not just ask better questions.</p>
<p class="big">They use psychology to reveal what different customers value, choose, and respond to.</p>
</div>
